    Concepts

    • AdditionAddition combines counts by repeated successor.
    • AlgorithmAn algorithm is a finite description of an effective step-by-step procedure for a class of inputs.
    • AttractorAn attractor is long-run structure toward which many permitted starting states move.
    • AxiomAn axiom is a declared starting statement or statement scheme of a formal theory.
    • Axiom of choiceA simultaneous choice can be made from every member of a family of nonempty sets.
    • Axiom of empty setThere exists a set with no members.
    • Axiom of extensionalityTwo sets are equal when they have exactly the same members.
    • Axiom of foundationEvery nonempty set has a member disjoint from it, blocking ordinary descending membership loops.
    • Axiom of infinityAt least one inductive set exists, supplying enough sets to model the natural numbers.
    • Axiom of pairingFor any two sets, a set exists whose members are exactly those two sets.
    • Axiom of power setFor every set, there is a set containing exactly all of its subsets.
    • Axiom of unionThe members of members of a set can be gathered into one set.
    • BijectionA bijection pairs two collections without omission or collision.
    • CardinalityCardinality compares collections by whether their elements can be paired exactly.
    • Category-theoretic foundationsCategory-theoretic foundations emphasize objects, composable arrows, and invariance under structure-preserving equivalence.
    • Chaos“Chaos” has several rigorous definitions. QEVA should name the definition being used instead of treating the word as self-explanatory.
    • ChiralityA chiral object has a handedness: mirroring changes it in a way that allowed orientation-preserving motions cannot undo.
    • Classical logicClassical logic is the branch that validates principles such as excluded middle and double-negation elimination.
    • Closed form“Closed form” usually means an explicit formula, but what operations are allowed differs by field and author.
    • Coarse-grainingCoarse-graining keeps distinctions relevant at one scale or task and merges others.
    • Collatz conjectureEvery tested starting value appears eventually to enter the 1→4→2→1 cycle, but no proof is known for all positive integers.
    • Collatz mapCollatz dynamics repeatedly applies one of two arithmetic rules depending on parity.
    • CompletenessCompleteness can mean that every semantic consequence is provable, or that a space has no missing limits; the meanings must be named.
    • Complex numberRepresent a complex number by a pair of real coordinates and define arithmetic so that the second coordinate behaves like a square root of minus one.
    • CompositionComposition feeds the output of one map into the input of another.
    • ComputabilityComputability asks which input-output tasks can be carried out by an idealized finite procedure.
    • ConjunctionConjunction joins requirements that must hold together.
    • ConsistencyA theory is consistent when its rules do not derive an explicit contradiction.
    • Constructive logicConstructive logic treats a proof as information and does not accept every classical principle without a construction.
    • ContinuityA continuous map does not tear apart the chosen topology: inverse images of observable open regions remain open.
    • DecidabilityA decision problem is decidable when one algorithm always halts and returns the correct yes/no answer.
    • DefinitionA definition fixes how a new expression is to be used in terms of already available structure.
    • Dependent type theoryDependent types may vary with terms, letting statements and proofs live in one typed language.
    • DerivabilityWriting Gamma |- P means that P can be reached by a finite sequence of allowed proof steps from the declared axioms and premises.
    • DerivativeA derivative is the best local linear rate of change when the relevant limit exists.
    • Discrete structureA discrete description treats states as individually separable rather than forcing arbitrarily close intermediate states.
    • DisjunctionDisjunction joins alternatives and says that at least one is admitted under the chosen logic.
    • DistinctionReasoning begins by allowing one state, mark, or object to be told apart from another.
    • Empty setThe empty set has no members. Its existence is theory-relative, and extensionality makes it unique when it exists.
    • Equivalence relationA relation is an equivalence relation when it behaves like equality with respect to reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity.
    • Existential quantifierExistential quantification asserts that at least one permitted witness satisfies a condition.
    • Exploration–exploitation tradeoffExploitation uses what currently looks best; exploration spends effort learning whether something else is better.
    • ExpressionAn expression is a finite arrangement of symbols built by explicit formation rules.
    • FieldA field is a commutative arithmetic system where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
    • First-order logicFirst-order logic quantifies over objects while keeping predicates and functions in a fixed signature.
    • Fixed pointA fixed point reproduces itself after one application of the update rule.
    • Formal systemA formal system fixes the symbols you may write, the starting statements you accept, and the rules by which new statements may be derived.
    • FunctionA function assigns exactly one output to each permitted input.
    • GraphA graph records objects and pairwise connections while discarding most other detail.
    • GroupA group captures reversible composition with an identity.
    • Group actionA group action describes how reversible transformations move objects while respecting composition.
    • Grouping / partitionGrouping makes some distinctions irrelevant by assigning multiple objects to the same class.
    • Halving“Half of x” is not one universal operation. It depends on what x is and which operations exist in its mathematical structure.
    • Hierarchy and scaleA hierarchical description says what belongs above, below, inside, or at a coarser scale—and how levels connect.
    • IdentityIdentity states that two references pick out the same object within a declared framework.
    • ImplicationImplication connects a condition to what follows from it.
    • Inference ruleAn inference rule licenses a transition from specified premises to a conclusion.
    • InjectionAn injective function never sends two different inputs to the same output.
    • IntegerIntegers extend natural numbers with additive opposites.
    • InvariantAn invariant deliberately forgets changes that the chosen transformations are allowed to make.
    • Law of excluded middleFor every statement P, classical logic admits P or not-P.
    • LimitA limit states that values eventually remain arbitrarily close to a target.
    • LinearityA linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
    • Local versus global optimumBeing unbeatable nearby does not mean being best everywhere.
    • Mathematical inductionInduction proves a property of every natural number from a base case and a successor step.
    • MeasureA measure assigns a nonnegative size to measurable sets while adding the sizes of disjoint pieces.
    • MembershipMembership records that an object is one of the elements of a set.
    • Metric spaceA metric assigns a distance satisfying nonnegativity, identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
    • ModelA model gives symbols a domain and interpretation so statements can be evaluated.
    • MultiplicationMultiplication combines equal-sized groups by repeated addition.
    • Natural numberFirst-order Peano arithmetic describes zero, successor, addition, multiplication, and induction through explicit axioms and schemas.
    • NegationNegation forms a statement that denies another statement under the chosen semantics.
    • NonlinearityIn a nonlinear system, combining inputs need not combine outputs by simple superposition.
    • ObjectAn object is whatever a chosen mathematical discourse permits us to refer to as one thing.
    • One plus one equals twoThe kernel expands addition once, then removes addition by zero, leaving exactly the term used to define two.
    • OperationAn operation takes inputs of declared kinds and returns an output of a declared kind; not every useful operation is closed on one set.
    • OptimizationOptimization first specifies which choices are allowed and how they are scored; the best lower score may or may not be achieved by a choice.
    • OrderAn order records a consistent notion of before, below, or no greater than.
    • Ordered pairAn ordered pair stores two objects while preserving which is first and which is second.
    • ParityAn integer is even when it is twice an integer and odd when it is one more than twice an integer.
    • Periodicity of a sequenceA periodic sequence repeats exactly after some fixed positive number of steps.
    • Prime numberA prime is greater than one and cannot be written as a product except using one or itself.
    • Probability spaceA probability space assigns normalized weight to measurable events.
    • ProofA proof is a finite, checkable chain from admitted premises to a conclusion under declared rules.
    • QuasiperiodicityA common quasiperiodic model combines several angular motions whose basic frequencies are rationally independent. The representation itself must be distinguished from the extra conditions needed to guarantee that the resulting function is nonperiodic.
    • Random variableA random variable converts outcomes into measurable values.
    • Rational numberRational numbers represent ratios of integers with nonzero denominator.
    • Real numberReal numbers complete the rationals so convergent measurement processes need not leave gaps.
    • Recurrence relationA recurrence describes how values are linked across index steps. It need not always determine a unique sequence unless enough initial data and uniqueness conditions are supplied.
    • RelationA relation records which tuples of objects stand in a chosen connection.
    • Riemann integralCut an interval into sufficiently short pieces, sample the function in each piece, and add height times width; one stable limiting value is the Riemann integral.
    • RingA ring supports addition, multiplication, and additive inverses under compatible laws.
    • SatisfactionA formula can be true in one mathematical structure and false in another. QEVA must name the semantics or model when it uses semantic truth.
    • Schema of replacementThe image of a set under a definable single-valued correspondence is a set.
    • Schema of separationA definable condition can select a subset of an already existing set.
    • Self-informationWithin a probability model, a less probable event carries more self-information when surprise is measured logarithmically.
    • Sensitive dependence on initial conditionsSensitivity formalizes one kind of error amplification: no matter how closely two starting states are chosen, some nearby state can eventually move a definite distance away.
    • SequenceA sequence is not merely a written list; mathematically it is a function whose input is an index.
    • SetA set is a collection treated extensionally: its members determine it.
    • Shannon entropyEntropy is the expected self-information of a random variable's distribution.
    • Sigma-algebraA sigma-algebra is a collection of events stable under complementation and countable combination.
    • Signal and noiseSignal is the part treated as informative for a task; noise is the part treated as nuisance, uncertainty, or unresolved variation.
    • StabilityA fixed point is Lyapunov-stable when starting close enough guarantees staying as close as requested forever.
    • StatementA statement is an expression eligible to be asserted, denied, proved, or evaluated in a model.
    • SubsetA is a subset of B when every member of A is also a member of B.
    • SuccessorSuccessor moves from one natural number to the next.
    • SurjectionA surjective function reaches every element of its declared codomain.
    • SymbolA symbol is an atomic mark or token admitted by a formal language.
    • SymmetrySymmetry is never just “looks the same”: one must specify which transformations are allowed and what counts as unchanged.
    • TheoremA theorem is a statement accompanied by a valid derivation from declared assumptions in a declared system.
    • Topological spaceA topology declares which regions count as open, encoding nearness without requiring numerical distance.
    • TypeA type classifies expressions and states which constructions may be formed with them.
    • Universal quantifierUniversal quantification requires a statement to hold for every permitted value in a domain.
    • Vector spaceA vector space supports vector addition and scalar multiplication under compatibility laws.
    • ZeroZero is the distinguished starting value for one common construction of the natural numbers.
    • ZFC set theoryZFC is a major foundational theory whose objects are sets governed by explicit axiom schemes and axioms.

    Experiments

    • Bounded Collatz orbitGenerate an exact finite Collatz trace and keep its limited evidential scope visible.
    • Coarse-grained signalHold a deterministic signal fixed while changing how many fine samples each observation combines.
    • Finite map cyclesEdit a finite transition rule and exhaustively expose its cycles, fixed points, and basins.
    • Local and exploratory searchCompare local improvement with seeded exploration on a fixed multi-peak landscape.
    • Logistic recurrence and sensitivityRun two nearby initial values under one recurrence and compare their finite-precision separation.
    • Modular equivalence classesChange the modulus and inspect which integer distinctions remain visible.
